item.title: Business License FAQ
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Business Licensing
Who needs to obtain a Vineyard Business License?

If someone is operating a business within the city limits, they are required to obtain a Vineyard Business License.  This includes home-based businesses.  The Vineyard Municipal Code Section 5.02.020 states:

5.02.020 Business License Required
It shall be a class B misdemeanor for any person to transact, engage in or carry on any business, trade, profession, calling or to operate a vending, pinball or coin-operated machine without first receiving the class or type of license required by the municipality.

Why are business licenses required?

Business licensing serves a real purpose in our community. Before the City issues a business license, the business must show that they are registered with the Utah Department of Commerce and have obtained any required county, state, or federal permits or licenses.  They also must have received approval from the Vineyard planning, fire, and building departments. 

Business licenses are required by law because they enable the city to:

  • Ensure public safety by enforcing building and fire codes
  • Verify that businesses are in compliance with the Vineyard Zoning Code and other laws and ordinances, such as state or county inspection requirements 
  • Collect its portion of sales tax revenue from the Utah State Tax Commission
  • Maintain a list of currently licensed businesses for public access
I have a business in my home. How do I know if I need a business license?
By law, all businesses, including home-based businesses, are required to have a business license. (The exception is that a business operated only occasionally by a person under the age of 18 is not required to have a license.) Please call the City office or visit the Business Licensing page.
What is the fee for a home-based business license?
Home offices with no impact on the neighborhood are not charged a fee for their license. See the Business License Application Portal for details. For other types of home-based businesses, the initial fee is $50 with an annual renewal fee of $25.
How long does it take to process a business license?
This depends on many factors, but some home offices take less than a week. Other businesses that need fire and building inspections, additional zoning review, or that need to change their state sales tax account to Vineyard will take longer. Please call the City office with any questions.
What about solicitors who knock on my door? Are they supposed to be licensed?

Yes. Every solicitor must have and wear a current Vineyard Solicitor’s License badge. A Solicitor's License is required to help ensure the safety of the citizens of Vineyard. Because the licensing process requires a background check on each individual solicitor, citizens can know that those who are coming to their homes selling products or services are individuals who have had a background check.

If a solicitor knocks on your door and you cannot clearly see their Vineyard Solicitors License badge, ask to see it. Please report to the Utah County Non-Emergency Dispatch number any solicitor going door to door without a license. 801-794-3970

item.title: Common Code Violations
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Occupancy
How many unrelated people can live in a house?
A total of four unrelated people can live in a home.  
Accessory Dwelling Units
Are ADUs allowed in Vineyard?
Yes, they are allowed in Vineyard if they meet the requirements listed in https://vineyard.municipalcodeonline.com/book?type=zoning#name=15.34.060_Accessory_Dwelling_Units.    
Where are ADUs allowed?
  • As a detached structure with at least 12,000 square foot lot  
  • Within a home, provided the lot is at least 5,200 square feet and meets all applicable building and fire codes
*Mobile homes, travel trailers, boats, or similar RVs are not permitted as an ADU 
What are the parking requirements for ADUs?
A single-family dwelling with an accessory dwelling unit shall provide a minimum of five (5) onsite parking spaces located on a paved surface or approved driveway.

Only driveways or parking pads containing a minimum length of eighteen feet (18’) may be counted toward required onsite parking. The minimum length of a driveway counting toward onsite parking shall not include any land associated with street rights-of-way, sidewalks, or public property/access.

All onsite parking spaces shall contain a minimum width of eight feet (8’). Property owner parking shall not be parked tandem with tenant parking, and tenant parking shall not be parked tandem with owner parking. The area dedicated to onsite parking and driveway surfaces shall be limited in compliance with VZC Section 15.38.030(2)(b).  
How many people can live in an ADU?
One family or up to four unrelated individuals may reside in an ADU.  
Parking
Can I park on the street?
While street parking is allowed, it is prohibited to leave any vehicle for 48 or more consecutive hours on the street at any time of year or when there is snow.  
Refuse
What is considered refuse?
  • Lumber, junk, trash, or debris
  • Abandoned, discarded, or unused objects or equipment, such as furniture, stoves, refrigerators, freezers, cans, or containers
When is refuse considered a nuisance?
Unsheltered storage of old, unused, stripped, and junked machinery, implements, equipment, or personal property of any kind that is no longer safely usable for the purposes for which it was manufactured for a period of 30 days or more (except in licensed junk yards) within this municipality is hereby declared to be a nuisance and dangerous to the public safety. 
Weeds
Why is maintaining weeds important?
Maintaining weeds helps stop the spread of seeds, which in turn helps lower the number of weeds growing in our city.

Keeping yards-maintained also helps encourage friendly, beautiful, and walkable neighbor- 
hoods. 
When would weeds be considered a nuisance?
Vineyard City requires that weeds be within 4 inches of the ground; anything over can be considered a nuisance. 
Recreational Vehicles
Where am I allowed to park my RV?
Recreational vehicles must be parked on the side or rear of the yard and screened from front yards by a fence. (Vineyard Zoning Code 15.34.100)   
Why am I not allowed to park my RV in the driveway or on the street?
This helps us guarantee that no sidewalks will be obstructed by trailers and that streets are clear from unnecessary trailers parked on the side of the streets.

item.title: Finance
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Sales Franchise Tax Debt Service Coverage

The payment for the Vineyard Center will fall within the range shown between the two charts below.  

Sales Franchise Tax Debt Service Coverage

Municipalities have several bond options to consider when funding building projects. These are three of the bonds Vineyard has considered:
  1. General Obligation (GO) Bonds – These bonds are backed by the full faith and credit of the city, meaning they are repaid through property taxes. Because they rely on taxpayer backing, they typically require voter approval and a property tax rate increase.
  2. Sales Tax Revenue Bonds – These bonds are repaid using revenue generated from city sales tax collections rather than property taxes. They do not require voter approval and are often a preferred choice for cities with strong commercial activity.
  3. Lease Revenue Bonds – These bonds are backed by lease payments from tenants occupying a facility. They are commonly used when a portion of a project is leased to private or public entities. This type of bond typically has a higher interest rate than GO or Sales Tax Revenue bonds. 

Choosing a Funding Approach

For the Vineyard Center, the city has opted for a Sales Tax Revenue Bond for several key reasons:

  • No tax increase – The bond will be repaid through the city’s existing and incoming sales tax revenue, meaning residents will not see an increase in their taxes.
  • Fixed interest rate – The bond’s interest rate will be locked in, protecting the city from market fluctuations.
  • Strong financial position – Vineyard has an excellent rating for this type of bond, thanks to the robust commercial growth across the city and in the new downtown area.

Looking at Cost Distribution and Sustainability

The financing of the Vineyard Center is structured as follows:

  • The Utah City Developer will donate the land on which the Vineyard Center will be built. 
  • Vineyard City will cover two-thirds of the total project cost.
  • Mountainland Association of Governments (MAG) will contribute approximately one-third of the cost.
  • A business incubator will lease space on the fourth floor creating a central hub for economic development in the city. Rent and lease revenue will support Vineyard’s portion of the bond repayment, ensuring a financially sustainable approach.

By leveraging a strategic mix of funding sources, Vineyard is making a smart investment in its future—enhancing services, supporting economic growth, and ensuring financial responsibility. The Vineyard Center will not only serve as a hub for government operations but also as a catalyst for further development and community engagement in our vibrant city.

item.title: Maintenance
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
As Vineyard City offers a robust and top-quality Open Space and Trails to its residents. And, in an effort to enhance the aesthetic appeal and usability of public spaces and facilities Vineyard City's initiative focuses on regular maintenance, beautification services, partnerships, and active volunteer involvement to elevate the quality of life for residents. Beyond promoting health through well-maintained parks and trails, the plan aims to establish Vineyard City as a unique and appealing place, fostering community connections in clean and inviting spaces. By instilling pride among residents, the city anticipates increased support for local government initiatives. The implementation involves a collaborative approach between the Public Works and Parks & Recreation departments, deploying trained staff to ensure cleanliness and health in public areas. Actively engaging the public in the preservation of open spaces and conducting regular surveys to gather feedback are integral components of the plan. As Vineyard City continues to grow, this initiative seeks to adapt open spaces in alignment with evolving community needs, ensuring a vibrant and sustainable environment for all residents.

Vineyard City established the Tree Manual to regulate urban forest health, aligning with the city's plan and codes. The objectives include maximizing canopy coverage, preventing conflicts with infrastructure, and promoting environmental benefits. The manual emphasizes proper tree placement, maintenance, and encourages similar practices on private property. It aims to create attractive landscaped spaces for public use while providing a standardized list of acceptable tree species for Vineyard's public areas.

"Designated as the Association of Government for our region, MAG strives to accomplish the best work we can for those we serve in Summit, Utah, and Wasatch County, Utah. We thrive on seeing the communities in our area grow and succeed. Our emphasis areas include Informed Aging, Community & Economic Development, and Planning for Growth."

Currently located in Orem and Vineyard, MAG approached Vineyard about locating the entirety of their services under one roof, in the new Vineyard Center. Their organization has outgrown their existing office space and they are eager to be part owners in the Vineyard Center project. As a financial partner, MAG is helping with the cost of design as well as construction for the building. With this partnership, both Vineyard City and MAG are able to cut down on expenses in shared use areas, such as break rooms, fitness centers, conference rooms, large training rooms, and storage rooms.

item.title: Ranked Choice Voting
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
What is Ranked Choice Voting?
Ranked choice voting or “Instant Run-Off Voting” allows voters to rank all of the candidates in order of preference when marking their ballots. Ranked choice voting eliminates the need for run-off elections. 

How do I mark the ranked choice voting ballot?
The ranked choice ballot card is designed in a side-by-side column format and lists the names of all of the candidates. This format allows a voter to select a first-choice candidate in the first column, a second-choice candidate in the second column, continuing until the voter is done ranking their preferred choices. 

How are ranked choice votes counted?
With ranked choice voting, if a candidate receives a majority (50%+1) of the first-choice votes cast for that office, that candidate will be elected. However, if no candidate receives a majority of the first-choice votes cast, an elimination process begins. The candidate who received the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated. Next, the voters whose first choice was cast for the eliminated candidate will have their second-choice vote cast in the second round. This elimination process will continue until one candidate receives a majority and is deemed the winner.

What if there are two open seats?
In an election with two open seats, such as a city council election, to elect the second seat, the second-choice vote of each voter whose vote was counted for a candidate already declared a winner will be counted for the second seat. The firs-choice vote of all other voters will be counted for the second seat. Rounds will continue until a second candidate has received more than half of the votes.  

If I really want my first-choice candidate to win, should I rank the candidate as my first, second and third choice?
No. Ranking a candidate more than once does not benefit the candidate. If a voter ranks one candidate as the voter's first, second and third choice, it is the same as if the voter leaves the second or third choice blank. In other words, if the candidate is eliminated, that candidate is no longer eligible to receive second or third choice votes. 

Can I give candidates the same ranking?
No. If a voter gives more than one candidate the same ranking, the ballot cannot be counted. Only one candidate can represent the voter's first, second, etc., choice. 

Can I write a candidate’s name on my ballot in any column?
Yes. In elections where there are qualified write-in candidates, there is a space provided to write in a name. Only qualified write-in candidates can receive votes.

 Does my vote still count if I only select one choice?
Yes. Your vote will count for your one choice.

What if I have further questions?
If you have further questions about ranked choice voting, please call the Vineyard City Recorder at 385-338-5183, or the Utah County Elections Office at 801-851-8128.

item.title: FAQs
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
General
What Is a Redevelopment Agency (RDA)?

A Redevelopment Agency (RDA) (also known as a Community Reinvestment Agency, or CRA) is a tool under state law that cities use to turn around neglected or industrial areas to foster investment, improve infrastructure and opportunity where private dollars wouldn’t otherwise go.

In Vineyard, we created the RDA in 2009 to help transform the former Geneva Steel Mill site—a large, contaminated and long-vacant industrial property—into a thriving, livable, and economically sustainable community.

Why Does Vineyard Need an RDA?

Without an RDA, Geneva would not have been transformed. Period.

The land was contaminated, vacant, and unattractive to investors. The RDA made it possible to:

  • Clean up environmental hazards
  • Build roads, water, and sewer systems
  • Support affordable housing and public parks
  • Attract major employers and institutions, such as UVU, Huntsman Cancer Institute, and Top Golf
  • Unlock billions in long-term investment and tax revenue
Without redevelopment, communities like Vineyard are left behind.
How Has the RDA Benefited Vineyard So Far?

Results:

  • Over 20,000 residents now call Vineyard home (up from ~100 in 1989).
  • Thousands of jobs have been created.
  • Major employers and institutions are now investing:
    • Huntsman Cancer Institute (with $22M in land donated by Flagborough Corp.)
    • Utah Valley University Vineyard Campus
    • Top Golf, Megaplex Theaters, Bella’s Market
  • Multifamily housing projects are adding millions in new property tax revenues.
  • Public infrastructure – roads, water lines, utilities – constructed without raising taxes.
All of this was made possible by the RDA. Without it, these investments would never have come.
What Would Not Have Been Built Today Without the RDA?
  • ALL Development North of Center
  • Top Golf and the Megaplex Theater
  • Huntsman Cancer Institute
  • Public infrastructure for roads, sewer, and utilities
  • Parks and community amenities
  • UVU’s campus access and education corridor

These projects required upfront public investment and risk that only an RDA could provide.

Is the RDA Accountable?

Absolutely. Vineyard’s RDA has:

  • Held public meetings and passed all funding through official board votes
  • Commissioned external CPA reviews (K&C CPAs) confirming no fraud or misuse
  • Acted swiftly to address technical accounting issues raised by the State Auditor
  • Launched transparency initiatives to rebuild trust and improve communication
  • No fraud, no mismanagement, no hidden spending
  • All expenditures aligned with adopted project plans and legally binding contracts
Is Vineyard’s RDA Successful?

Yes, it is one of the most successful redevelopment efforts in the state of Utah.

From industrial ruin to a thriving, modern city, the RDA has:

  • Sparked billions in investment
  • Created jobs and housing
  • Expanded the region’s tax base
  • Preserved educational funding
  • Built a foundation for the next 100 years of Vineyard’s growth

The following chart shows the taxable value of land in Vineyard’s RDA project area (Phases 3 & 4) compared to:

  • A nearby residential area not in the RDA area (The Homesteads)
  • Agricultural land in residential and commercial zones in nearby American Fork that has remained undeveloped
  • A scenario where the Geneva site had never been redeveloped

The difference is clear: the area in the RDA increased the tax base more than non-RDA areas, —making land more valuable, productive, and beneficial for the entire region.

Is the RDA Sustainable?

Yes. The RDA is designed to sunset after key goals are met. When that happens:

  • 100% of all property taxes revert to the school district and other taxing entities
  • The area continues to thrive from the permanent infrastructure already in place
  • Vineyard and its partners will see compounded returns for decades
When did Geneva Steel close?
The steel plant closed in 2001 after declaring bankruptcy. The Geneva Steel facility was constructed by the Defense Plant Corporation, an arm of the federal government in 1912. It was purchased in 1946 by USX Corporation (USX), United States Steel Division (USS). Geneva Steel acquired the facility in 1987 and operated the facility until 2001 until declaring bankruptcy. In 2005 Anderson Geneva LLC, and affiliates purchased the land from the Geneva Steel bankruptcy estate and now manage the Site deconstruction, remediation, and redevelopment.  The Bankruptcy trustee sold the steel making equipment to Qingdao Iron and Steel Group Co., Ltd. of China. Qingdao disassembled and removed all of its purchased equipment and completed its work in early 2006. CST Environmental, Inc. purchased the salvage rights from the bankruptcy estate in December 2004 with the requirement to demolish all of the buildings and structures to grade level.
Who is in charge of cleanup of the former steel mill site?
Anderson Geneva is the permitted party responsible for environmental cleanup.
Under federal environmental laws including the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA), the EPA works with state environmental regulators (Utah Department of Environmental Quality, DEQ) to regulate, permit, and oversee environmental remediation and cleanup (“corrective action”) for sites like former steel mills that contain hazardous solid waste. In the case of the former Geneva Steel mill site, a Utah Hazardous Waste Post-Closure Permit was issued to United States Steel Corporation (USS) and the purchaser of the property Anderson Geneva, LLC for post-closure care and facility-wide corrective action for dealing with the waste and debris leftover after closure of the steel mill. This is a highly regulated process which requires complex planning and approvals by the state and federal government and ongoing testing, reporting, tracking, and compliance for a myriad of clean-up activities. This permit was issued in 2004 and updated in 2010. The former mill site has been issued an EPA ID (EPA RCRA ID: UTD009086133) and cleanup progress is closely monitored to comply with all state and federal environmental laws. Cleanup at the site is still ongoing under the permit issued to Anderson Geneva who regularly reports required information to the Utah DEQ.
School
Does the RDA Take Money Away From Schools?

No. This is a critical misconception that must be corrected:

  • Schools keep 100% of the tax dollars they were already getting before the RDA began.
  • Only 75% of new growth dollars are temporarily reinvested.
  • The Alpine School District voluntarily participates in Vineyard’s RDA through a formal Taxing Entity Committee.
  • At the end of the RDA term, schools will permanently receive much more revenue due to increased property values.
Example: Alpine School District has already received substantial new funds from developments like the movie theater and Top Golf, none of which would exist without the RDA.

This chart shows the school’s 25% share of incremental tax dollars on top of the base tax revenues from the original undeveloped land values. The revenue for schools has grown significantly thanks to development.
How Does This Help Students?

Students benefit in multiple ways:

  • Increased future tax base = more long-term funding for education
  • Access to higher education and research through UVU and Huntsman Institute
  • Safer neighborhoods, more housing, and community amenities
  • Expansion of services and quality of life that help families thrive
Finance
Where Does the RDA Money Come From?

The RDA uses a system called Tax Increment Financing (TIF),  which reinvests future property tax revenue growth into redevelopment, not existing public budgets.

The base value of the property is frozen (in Vineyard’s case, extremely low due to the Geneva blight). As new development raises property values, the increase (or “increment”) in tax revenue is reinvested into public improvements in the area.

These funds are not new taxes – they are growth-driven dollars, which would not exist without redevelopment.

This chart shows the model in Utah for how tax increment financing works:

This chart shows the actual data for Vineyard since the RDA began. As redevelopment has occurred, the taxable value of the area has increased almost 9x resulting in participating tax entities receiving quadruple the tax revenue they would have received had no redevelopment occurred:

Does Tax Increment Financing raise your taxes?
The use of tax increment financing (TIF) in the context of community reinvestment in Utah (RDA, URA, CRA) is not designed with the intent of increasing taxes on individual property taxpayers. Rather, this financing tool re-directs the additional tax revenue from new development for a period of time to use this increased "new growth" revenue to pay for the infrastructure and costs related to redeveloping previously blighted properties. This functions as a deferral of "new growth" revenue from an earlier year to a later year in order to reinvest that new growth revenue to pay for, on a "post-performance" basis, the public costs of redevelopment (like infrastructure).

What this means for the former Geneva steel mill industrial site and the Geneva Urban Renewal Area (Vineyard RDA) is that the vacant and blighted industrial land, after the demolition of the steel mill, is assessed a base value after the demolition. The tax revenue from that base value land continues to go to all local tax entities. The increased value of the land as redevelopment occurs produces new "incremental" tax revenue (essentially "new growth" tax revenue). This additional or incremental tax revenue is then used to pay back the costs of the infrastructure development that facilitated and made possible that increased tax value. A 75% portion of this "incremental revenue" is given to the RDA to pay for these costs after the development has occurred. A 25% share of this incremental revenue still flows to the local government taxing entities. After the increment time period (typically 25 years), all the new tax revenue then goes to the local government entities thus increasing the "new growth" at that time.
 
The reason this tool is designed in this way is that it would be infeasible for a local government to pay for infrastructure to develop blighted or vacant land since that local government doesn't have significant property tax revenue from that land to fund infrastructure. In the case of Vineyard, the vacant industrial steel mill site no longer produced significant property tax revenue for the city such that the city could not raise capital or obtain bonds to build roads or utility systems that makes development possible. However, if the city could immediately finance the creation of roads and utilities, then developers could actually build homes, commercial and industrial developments which would then produce property tax revenue. Tax increment financing makes it possible to do this quickly rather than having that vacant land languish for many years.

item.title: Plan Progress
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Development
Former Geneva Steel Mill Site
Images of the project area from 2009 to 2025 show the significant progress of development as well as the work left to be done in preparing the industrial site for future development.

Image: https://drive.google.com/file/d/18-UHnkH4hL1JVO7mu9iCeT54CH0x-EgV/view?usp=sharing
Environmental Remediation
Anderson Geneva is the permitted party responsible for environmental cleanup. Under federal environmental laws including the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA), the EPA works with state environmental regulators (Utah Department of Environmental Quality, DEQ) to regulate, permit, and oversee environmental remediation and cleanup (“corrective action”) for sites like former steel mills that contain hazardous solid waste. In the case of the former Geneva Steel mill site, a Utah Hazardous Waste Post-Closure Permit was issued to United States Steel Corporation (USS) and the purchaser of the property Anderson Geneva, LLC for post-closure care and facility-wide corrective action for dealing with the waste and debris leftover after closure of the steel mill. This is a highly regulated process which requires complex planning and approvals by the state and federal government and ongoing testing, reporting, tracking, and compliance for a myriad of clean-up activities. This permit was issued in 2004 and updated in 2010. The former mill site has been issued an EPA ID (EPA RCRA ID: UTD009086133) and cleanup progress is closely monitored to comply with all state and federal environmental laws. Cleanup at the site is still ongoing under the permit issued to Anderson Geneva who regularly reports required information to the Utah DEQ.

One feature of corrective action was construction of a consolidated (or corrected action) area management unit (CAMU):

  • Moving impacted soil into a membrane-covered structure.
  • Overall Work Area (Eastside) - Approximately 400 acres
  • Site Preparation - Approximately 1.2 million cubic yards
  • CAMU Embankment - Approximately 550,000 cubic yards
  • CAMU Area - 33 acres
  • CAMU Height - 46 Feet
  • CAMU Storage Capacity - Approximately 800,000 cubic yards
  • Liner Materials - Approximately 4 Million square feet
  • Final Cover / Cap Materials - Approximately 100,000 cubic yards
  • Interim Grading - Approximately 300,000 cubic yards
Tax Base
Expanding a Diverse Tax Base for Schools and Local Government
The plan calls for increasing sales tax revenue and expanding the tax base by enhancing property values across diverse types of development.
Vineyard City General Fund Revenues
Since the beginning of the project, the tax revenues for Vineyard city have grown with significant increases in sales tax. This is a significant benefit to the area as it reduces the individual tax burden on residents and homeowners through property tax alone. This is a chart of all city general fund revenues over time broken out in property tax, sales tax, and all others. The others includes Other taxes (RAP, Transportation, Franchise), licenses, permits, intergovernmental, charges for service, fines, and interest.
Property Values
The intended purpose of RDA’s and the use of tax increment financing is to encourage redevelopment of blighted areas so that the land and property is more economically viable to attract investment and new uses including new businesses and residents. This causes the property to become more valuable which in turn increases property tax revenues for the participating tax entities. The success of the RDA can be measured in the magnitude and speed of the increase in taxable land values.

Since the plan’s adoption in 2011, the increase in property values has been very strong and has even outpaced original estimates in the planned forecast by 45%. This is a significant growth in value over the base value of the blighted land before the project began.
Taxable Value for Taxing Entities
The Plan aims to increase taxable values for participating taxing entities to increase the total property tax revenues as new properties are developed. This chart shows the increase in total taxable value broken down by the share that taxing entities would benefit from for their 25% share of tax increment financing as compared to the base value. Taxing entities have benefitted greatly from the rapid development yielding more tax revenue than if the site had not been developed.
School Tax Revenues
Schools keep 100% of the tax dollars they were already getting before the RDA began. This is the tax revenue from the “base” values of the property as set in 2006. 75% of the new growth dollars are then temporarily reinvested to fund infrastructure in the redevelopment project area. At the end of the tax increment term, schools will permanently receive much more revenue due to increased property values.

This chart shows the school’s 25% share of incremental tax dollars on top of the base tax revenues from the original undeveloped land values. The revenue for schools has grown significantly thanks to development.
Taxable Values Compared to Alternative Scenarios
What if Vineyard never created an RDA for the former Geneva site? Property values have changed in the redevelopment project area compared to raw land values in the surrounding community and other nearby housing developments.

This chart shows a comparison of the Geneva “brownfield” site to a nearby parcel of 40 acres of undeveloped land in American Fork that is currently being leased for agriculture use and taxed under the agricultural “green belt” exemption. Redevelopment has increased the tax base faster than the rate of value growth in land alone. The tax revenue for developed areas far exceeds the tax revenue from greenbelt land.

The following chart shows the taxable value of land in Vineyard’s RDA project area (Phases 3 & 4) compared to:

  • A nearby residential area not in the RDA area (The Homesteads)
  • Agricultural land in residential and commercial zones in nearby American Fork that has remained undeveloped
  • A scenario where the Geneva site had never been redeveloped

The difference is clear: the area in the RDA increased the tax base more than non-RDA areas, —making land more valuable, productive, and beneficial for the entire region.
New Retailers
A variety of significant new retailers, restaurants, and other businesses have located in Vineyard due to the redevelopment plan.
    1. 2015: Megaplex opened a movie theater. 
    2. 2023: TopGolf opened their second Utah location in Vineyard.
    3. 2025: the first grocery store, Bella’s Market will open.
Job Creation
Increase Jobs With a Wide Range of Skills
The Project Plan calls for creating a large number of jobs with a wide range of skill levels.
Huntsman Cancer Institute
In 2025, the Huntsman Cancer Institute broke ground on a new 272,000 square foot hospital to be located in the new Utah City development in downtown Vineyard development. Huntsman Cancer Institute’s Comprehensive Cancer Center will open to patients in fall 2028.
National Impact
National Job Creators
The Plan aims to attract national tenants and other job creators looking to build in the Mountain West. A number of significant companies with regional significance have already located or announced locations in the redevelopment site including the new Huntsman Cancer Institute.
Transportation
Alternative Transportation Hubs
The Plan seeks to make possible alternative transportation hubs to minimize congestion and improve air quality:

“The Geneva Urban Renewal Area will… lay the framework for a more pedestrian and transit-oriented city… and facilitate the redevelopment of the surrounding area”...“There are currently no public infrastructure improvements within the majority of the Project Area. The construction of the public infrastructure improvements... will support the development contemplated by this Plan” and “Take advantage of the proximity to Utah Lake and the planned future transit station… and create an intermodal hub transit area and offer transportation corridors.”

Work has progressed to successfully bring a commuter rail station to Vineyard and plans are ongoing to add bus and light rail service as well.
  • Center St & 300 W rail crossings complete
  • Vineyard Connector arterial road established
  • Rail spur relocation for future Frontrunner station access
Housing and Transit Reinvestment Zone (HTRZ)
Vineyard was approved for an HTRZ designation which allows a portion of state sales tax revenue to be used in developing the area near the UTA Frontrunner station with housing that is accessible to transit.
Housing
A Variety of Housing Types
The Plan calls for a variety of housing types for a wide range of income levels. Thus far, over 3,800 residential housing units have been constructed and the city’s population has grown significantly (as of 2024).
  • 20+ neighborhoods built: Waters Edge, Lakefront, The Forge, Vineyard Shores
  • Zoning mix includes townhomes, single-family, and multi-family
Population Growth
As a result of significant growth in available housing in the city from the project, many residents have been able to make their homes in Vineyard. The city has been frequently recognized as one of the fastest growing in the US.
Regional Impact
Encouraging Additional Development Regionally
The Project Plan calls for encouraging additional development on the perimeter of the redevelopment area.
Community
Sustainable Community
The plan aims to create a sustainable community.
Public Recreation Spaces
Vineyard has many excellent public spaces, parks and venues for recreation. The new Greenline Promenade will be a multi-acre green space with thousands of trees and connected parks.

item.title: Project Plan
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
The Geneva Urban Renewal Area follows the adopted Project Area Plan adopted in 2011. The Project Plan outlines 8 major purposes for redevelopment of the site:

  1. Make possible the redevelopment of over 2,055 acres of under-utilized real estate which has been contaminated and blighted due to over a half century of heavy industrial use. 
  2. Provide the basis for enhanced property and sales tax revenues for the Town, County, School District, other taxing entities and State. 
  3. Create a large number of jobs with a wide range of skill levels. 
  4. Attract national tenants and other job creators looking to build in the Mountain West. 
  5. Make possible alternative transportation hubs to minimize congestion and improve air quality.
  6. Provide a variety of housing types for a wide range of income levels. 
  7. Encourage additional development on the perimeter of the redevelopment area. 
  8. Create a sustainable community.

item.title: Road Maintenance
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded: The city streets division is tasked with the critical responsibility of maintaining the road infrastructure within the municipality. Their duties encompass a wide range of activities to preserve road safety and functionality. This includes promptly repairing potholes, resurfacing roads to prevent deterioration, sealing cracks to minimize water damage, and repainting markings for visibility. Additionally, they remove snow and ice during winter, ensuring safe passage for vehicles and pedestrians. Routine tasks such as sign maintenance, street sweeping, and conducting inspections to identify maintenance needs are also part of their responsibilities. Through these efforts, the city streets division is vital in facilitating efficient transportation and enhancing the overall quality of life for residents and commuters alike.

item.title: Wastewater & Sewer Services
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded: Vineyard City's Sewer and Wastewater Treatment services provide a comprehensive plan to manage and treat sewage effectively. The city focuses on ensuring compliance with environmental regulations, maintaining public health standards, and promoting sustainable practices. Vineyard City's Public Works staff provides for sewer collection for all the residents and businesses in the city, utilizing three pump stations to send the sewage to the wastewater treatment facility. Public Works partners with Timpanogos Special Service District (TSSD) to provide for the treatment processes for wastewater, emphasizing the use of advanced technologies to safeguard water quality. This program measures to prevent pollution, reduce environmental impact, and optimize the efficiency of the sewer system. Vineyard City initiative is a commitment to responsible wastewater management, safeguarding the community's well-being and the environment.

item.title: Site Design
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Working through a competitive bid process, Method Studios was selected from a pool of 16 architectural firms to design the Vineyard Center. Method has demonstrated their talent in designing familiar buildings such as: Orem City Hall, The Ruth, The Noorda Center for the Performing Arts, and many other projects throughout the state. You can view their projects here.

Design work for the Vineyard Center began in 2022 with a spatial analysis from Nelson Partners to determine how much space was needed to accommodate Vineyard City and MAG. It was determined that a 4 story building located on Block 10A of the Utah City Development would be sufficient for this project. From that spatial analysis, Method Studio has been working on refining it and designing a building that will meet staff and community needs. 

One unique aspect of this project is the building location. Flagborough donated 1.25 acres to Vineyard City right off of the Promenade Park set to open in Summer of 2025. The ground floor of the Vineyard Center is being designed in a way to essentially expand the park onto the ground floor of the building. There will be space for public markets, community meeting rooms, and other community services.

item.title: Snow Removal
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
When inclement winter weather hits, the Vineyard City Public Works department is hard at work clearing our streets for safer travel. Our priority is to make all main roads passable for safety vehicles – this means streets receive a higher priority according to volume of traffic, proximity to schools or public buildings, steepness of grade, etc.

As long as the snow continues to fall, our first goal is to keep high priority roads clear. In such instances, it is unlikely that residential roads will be reached immediately because the main roads must be repeatedly plowed. After the main roads are cleared, we are able to move to residential streets followed by cul-de-sacs and dead-ends.

Vineyard residents also play a role in helping to keep roads and sidewalks free of snow and ice. Please keep the following points in mind.

The following actions are not allowed:
  • Blowing or pushing snow into any public street.
  • Parking on city streets during a snowstorm or whenever snow is present.
  • The Sheriff’s department is authorized to cite residents if they are not in compliance with any ordinance.
Homeowners responsibilities:
  • Removing snow in front of your mailbox once plows have been through the neighborhood.
  • Clearing snow from sidewalks in front of their homes within 24 hours of a storm.
  • If there is a fire hydrant in front of a resident’s home, they must clear it of all snow.
  • Clearing snow from driveway approaches. Snow accumulated on the plow blade has no place to go but in the right-of-way, which includes driveway approaches.

The City possesses neither the personnel nor equipment to clear thousands of driveway approaches within the City. If possible, please assist the elderly and infirm neighbors.

Public Works after-hours emergency line: (435) 228-5083

item.title: Stormwater
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
STORM WATER MANAGEMENT
For public comment concerning storm water management please email the Vineyard storm water division.

GOAL OF THE DIVISION
The goal of Vineyard's storm water division is to reduce the amount of pollution entering our waterways through storm water runoff. This will ensure the health of our local waterways and help provide clean drinking water and safe and beautiful lakes and waterways for recreation. As a side benefit storm water pollution prevention also helps maintain clean streets and in conjunction with low impact development practices can help recharge aquifers which ensures our drinking water supply into the future.

STORM WATER METHODS
Keeping the storm water clean is achieved through 2 main methods, either by the use of storm water pollution prevention plans (SWPPP) on construction sites or municipal cleaning activities. The use of a SWPPP and permit is required for any development 1 acre or larger, or any development smaller than 1 acre that is part of a larger development. Municipal activities include storm drain cleaning, trash pickup, and monitoring all town facilities for possible sources of pollution. The other 4 areas of storm water management are public education, public involvement, illicit discharge detection and elimination and post-construction management.

24 HOUR ILLICIT DISCHARGE DETECTION & ELIMINATION HOTLINE
Please call 385-625-7071 if you witness any illegal discharge of contaminants into the storm water system, including: Excessive construction track-out Hazardous material spills Illegal dumping

item.title: Stormwater & Floodplain Management
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Stormwater & Floodplain Management

Stormwater is rainwater or snowmelt that flows over streets, sidewalks, parking lots, and other surfaces instead of soaking into the ground. As it travels, it can carry pollutants such as oil, trash, fertilizers, and pet waste into local waterways.

Floodplain management focuses on reducing flood risks by protecting areas that are prone to flooding and promoting responsible development. Together, stormwater and floodplain management help protect our community, improve water quality, reduce flooding, and preserve our natural resources for future generations.

Explore the sections above to learn how Vineyard City manages stormwater, protects waterways, and how you can help keep our community clean and safe!

Report a Spill or Illicit Discharge
Vineyard City is committed to protecting our waterways and complying with Utah’s UPDES Permit UTR090000. If you witness or suspect any unauthorized dumping, spills, or other illicit discharges into our storm drains, creeks, or open ditches, please let us know immediately. Your report helps us keep our community and environment safe!

How to Report
Call our dedicated Public Works hotline:
(801) 226-1929
(Monday–Thursday, 8:00 am–5:00 pm; Friday, 8:00 am–12:00 pm)

Our Location & Office Hours
Vineyard City
125 S Main St
Vineyard, UT 84059

Office Hours:

AFTER HOURS WATER & SEWER EMERGENCIES
For spills, discharges, or other environmental/water quality concerns that occur after 5 pm Monday - Thursday or after noon on Fridays and on the weekends, please contact: 
(801)226-1929

Thank you for helping keep Vineyard City’s stormwater system clean and our environment healthy. A written record is kept of all calls received, all follow-up actions taken, and any feedback received from public education efforts. We use your reports and our response data to:

  • Refine our public education and outreach efforts
  • Update best-management practices
  • Track trends and reduce future incidents

If you have questions or need more information, please contact us at (801) 226-1929 or visit our office during regular business hours.

item.title: Construction Stormwater Manageme
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Protecting Water Quality During Construction

Construction activities can increase the amount of sediment, debris, and pollutants that enter the storm drain system. Vineyard City works with contractors and developers to ensure best management practices (BMPs) are used to protect local waterways throughout construction projects.

Proper stormwater management helps prevent erosion, reduces pollution, and protects our community and Utah Lake.

Stormwater Best Management Practices (BMPs)

Construction sites should implement practices such as:

  • Installing erosion and sediment controls
  • Protecting storm drains from sediment and debris
  • Stabilizing disturbed soil
  • Properly storing construction materials
  • Managing concrete washout areas
  • Preventing pollutants from leaving the construction site

Construction Stormwater Resources

Our Construction Stormwater Management brochure provides guidance on stormwater requirements, pollution prevention, and best management practices for construction sites.

📄 Download the Construction Stormwater Management Brochure

Report a Construction Stormwater Concern

If you observe sediment, muddy runoff, or other pollutants leaving a construction site, please let us know.

Examples include:

  • Mud or sediment washing into streets or storm drains
  • Poor erosion control measures
  • Construction debris entering waterways
  • Concrete washout in unauthorized areas
  • Other stormwater pollution concerns

Contact Public Works Department
Kinsli McDermott
MS4 Coordinator | Vineyard City
stormwater@vineyardutah.gov

item.title: Long-Term Stormwater Management
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Protecting Our Community for the Future

Stormwater management doesn't end when construction is complete. Long-term stormwater management helps ensure that drainage systems, ponds, swales, and other stormwater facilities continue to function properly for years to come.

Routine maintenance and inspections help protect water quality, reduce flooding, and preserve the health of our community and Utah Lake.


Stormwater facilities are designed to:

  • Reduce flooding
  • Improve water quality
  • Prevent erosion
  • Capture sediment and pollutants
  • Protect local waterways and Utah Lake

Regular maintenance helps these systems continue working as intended.


Maintaining Stormwater Facilities

Stormwater systems require ongoing care to remain effective. Maintenance activities may include:

  • Inspecting stormwater facilities
  • Removing sediment and debris
  • Maintaining drainage channels and swales
  • Cleaning storm drains and catch basins
  • Repairing damaged infrastructure
  • Managing vegetation around stormwater facilities


Everyone Plays a Role

Property owners, businesses, developers, and the City all play an important role in protecting stormwater infrastructure.

You can help by:

  • Keeping storm drains free of leaves and debris.
  • Properly disposing of trash and household chemicals.
  • Never dumping anything into storm drains.
  • Reporting damaged or clogged stormwater facilities.


Report a Stormwater Concern

If you notice a damaged storm drain, blocked drainage channel, or other stormwater issue, please let us know.

Examples include:

  • Clogged storm drains
  • Damaged catch basins
  • Flooding or drainage issues
  • Excessive sediment buildup
  • Damaged stormwater facilities


Contact Public Works Department
Kinsli McDermott
MS4 Coordinator | Vineyard City
stormwater@vineyardutah.gov

item.title: Pollution Prevention & Good Housekeeping
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
What Is Pollution Prevention?

Pollution prevention means stopping pollutants before they reach the storm drain system. Since stormwater flows directly to local waterways without treatment, preventing pollution is one of the most effective ways to protect water quality.




Our Public Works Department helps prevent stormwater pollution by:

  • Sweeping streets to remove dirt, leaves, and debris
  • Cleaning and maintaining storm drains and catch basins
  • Inspecting stormwater facilities
  • Maintaining parks, trails, and public spaces
  • Properly storing and handling maintenance materials
  • Training employees on stormwater best management practices (BMPs)
  • Responding to spills and stormwater concerns

How You Can Help

Everyone plays a role in protecting our waterways. You can help by:

  • Never dumping anything into storm drains
  • Picking up pet waste
  • Properly disposing of motor oil, paint, and household chemicals
  • Keeping leaves, grass clippings, and trash out of gutters
  • Washing vehicles at a commercial car wash or on grassy areas when appropriate
  • Reporting spills or illegal dumping

Every small action helps keep Vineyard's waterways clean.

Great Resources!
Utah Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ)

Household Hazardous Waste
Learn how to properly dispose of paint, motor oil, batteries, pesticides, and other household hazardous waste to prevent pollution.

Hazardous Waste Management Program
Information for businesses and organizations on hazardous waste management, pollution prevention, and compliance.

There are many simple ways to make a positive impact:

  • Pick up litter in your neighborhood or local park.
  • Properly dispose of pet waste.
  • Keep leaves, grass clippings, and debris out of storm drains.
  • Report illegal dumping or stormwater pollution.
  • Volunteer during community cleanup events.
  • Share stormwater education with your family and neighbors.

Community Cleanups

Vineyard City periodically hosts community cleanup opportunities that help keep our streets, parks, trails, and waterways clean. These events are a great way to get involved while making a positive impact in our community.

Check our Events Calendar for upcoming cleanup opportunities!

Report a Stormwater Concern

If you see anything that could impact stormwater quality, please let us know.

Examples include:

  • Illegal dumping
  • Oil or chemical spills
  • Clogged storm drains
  • Flooding concerns
  • Construction site runoff

Contact
Kinsli McDermott
MS4 Coordinator | Vineyard City
stormwater@vineyardutah.gov

Every Action Matters

Small actions can have a big impact. By keeping pollutants out of storm drains and participating in community efforts, you help protect local waterways and preserve Vineyard's natural beauty.

Only rain belongs down the drain!

What Is Stormwater?

Stormwater is rainwater or snowmelt that flows over rooftops, streets, parking lots, and other surfaces instead of soaking into the ground. As it travels, it can pick up pollutants such as oil, fertilizer, pet waste, litter, and chemicals. Unlike wastewater, stormwater is not treated before it enters storm drains, which flow directly to local waterways. By working together to keep stormwater clean, we help protect our community, wildlife, and Utah Lake for future generations.

Did you know? Stormwater isn't treated before it reaches local waterways.

UCA 20A-16-502 May 1, 2025

Dear Voter,

This notice pertains to voters covered under the Uniformed and Overseas Absentee Voting Act (UOCAVA) that are eligible to vote in the upcoming election.

This is a municipal election year and Vineyard, Utah will have one mayoral seat and three council seats up for election (four-year terms with one exception see our initial election notice for details.) Utah County will be gaining a new city: Spring Lake, Utah. There will be an election for their mayor and city council seats. Alpine School District (ASD) will also be splitting into 3 school boards. If you are part of the ASD, you will also have your new school board seat on your ballot.

For information on the ASD split or the new city election, reach out to the Elections Office.

Last day to request a ballot: 8/11/2025
Postmark deadline: 8/11/2025

Electronic ballots must be received by the Elections Oﬃce by 8:00 PM (Mountain Standard Time) on Election Day, Tuesday, August 12, 2025. Mailed ballots must be postmarked no later than the day before Election Day, Monday, August 11, 2025, and received up through the Election Canvass. For more information on the use of the Federal Post Card Application (FPCA), the Federal Voting Assistance Program (fvap.gov), and related deadlines, or the use of a Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot (FWAB), please visit Utah County Election Division website at vote.utahcounty.gov. item.title: Traffic Calming
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
OBJECTIVES
  • Improve safety for all users of the streets
  • Recognize the right of the public to use the street
  • Promote safe and pleasant conditions for motorists, bicyclists, pedestrians, and residents
  • Encourage citizen involvement in all aspects of the three E’s of Traffic Calming: Education, Enforcement, and Engineering
WHAT IS TRAFFIC CALMING?
Traffic calming is the desired outcome of using a combination of public and city measures to include traffic devices to regulate traffic and reduce the negative effects of motor vehicle use. This involves changing the look and feel of residential streets to lower vehicle speeds, alter driver behavior, and improve safety for pedestrians and cyclists. These devices are not meant to divert traffic, but to slow traffic to an appropriate speed when within local streets. Examples of traffic calming devices include speed humps, raised pedestrian crosswalks, lane reduction, narrow lanes, traffic circles, traffic medians, speed radar signs, and on-street parking.

THE THREE E’S OF TRAFFIC CALMING
The three E’s of traffic calming emphasize the integral role every member of the community has when it comes to improving road safety.
1. Education- It is everyone’s responsibility to be aware of and follow the rules of the road to ensure safe practices and ease traffic issues.
2. Enforcement- Utah County Sheriff’s Office provides law enforcement efforts to encourage safe behaviors.
3. Engineering- Vineyard City Engineering works with Developers to incorporate effective traffic calming devices into designs of new developments and works with residents and other agencies regarding enhancing existing infrastructure.

WHAT CAN YOU DO?
There are several things residents can do to reduce speeding issues, such as the following:
  1.  Talk to your neighbors and make them aware of the speeding problem
  2. Confirm that those living/visiting your household do not contribute to the problem
  3. Collaborate with City Council to create a community-wide awareness program
  4. Ask the Sheriff/Sheriff’s representative at City Council to increase enforcement of your roadway
  5. Work together with your neighbors to implement ideas that make front yards, sidewalks, and streets friendly to pedestrians, bicyclists, and kids playing.
TRAFFIC CALMING REQUEST
For Traffic Calming requests please fill out the contact form below or contact Vineyard City’s Engineering Department at engineering@vineyardutah.org

item.title: Voter Information
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
How do I register to vote?
If you have not registered to vote and want to vote in the primary election and want to vote in the primary election, please go to the Utah County Elections Office by Monday August 11, at 5:00 PM or any vote center on Tuesday August 12, 2025 from 7:00 AM to 8:00 PM.  Please visit vote.utahcounty.gov to find a location near you.

If you are not registered, please visit the state website  before October 24, 2025 to vote in the Municipal General Election. You may also register in person at the Utah County Clerk's Office, which is located at: 100 E Center Street, Room 3100, Provo, UT 84606.

  • We recommend that you register EARLY to receive your ballot in the mail. If you do not receive your mailed ballot you can vote provisionally on Election Day. Vineyard will not have a Ballot Pickup/Vote Center. Please check the county website for locations. 
  • An individual who is not registered to vote may register to vote and vote during the early voting period. 

What if I have moved?
To update your voter registration:

  • Log on to vote.utah.gov or
  • Register in person at the Utah County Clerk's Office Monday through Friday at 100 E Center Street, Room 3100, Provo, UT.
  • Call the Utah County Clerk's Office at 801.851.8128 to change your address on your voter registration.
  • Please be aware that in order to vote in Vineyard, you must establish residency in Utah at least 30 days before Election Day and live in Vineyard at the time of the election. 

Deadlines to establish residency:

  • Primary Election, if necessary: July 13, 2025
  • General Election: October 5, 2025
What if I am temporarily living out of state?
This would be for those who move away for the winter, are in the military, living overseas, or are missionaries:

When registering to vote at vote.utah.gov make sure you put the temporary address as the mailing address.  

For those who might be transferred during the election period, make sure you update your mailing address.

Missionaries: we recommend that you use your mission home address as the mailing address.

item.title: Water Conservation
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Utah's water conservation efforts focus on efficient irrigation, public awareness, and technology adoption to ensure sustainable water use. The state prioritizes proactive water management, addressing scarcity through innovation and community engagement for long-term sustainability.

Utah Division of Water Resources provides a weekly lawn watering guide to help you know when to water!
https://conservewater.utah.gov/guide.html 
 
Visit Central Utah Gardens for activities and educational classes about water conservation.
http://centralutahgardens.org 
 
Central Utah Water Conservancy District (CUWCD) rebate program
http://rebates.cuwcd.com/
 

The Water Conservation Plan for Vineyard City in 2022 outlines comprehensive strategies to promote responsible water usage and ensure sustainable water resources for the community. The plan focuses on various conservation measures, including efficient irrigation practices, public awareness campaigns, and the implementation of water-saving technologies. It addresses both short-term and long-term goals, emphasizing the importance of community engagement and collaboration. The document reflects Vineyard City's commitment to proactive water management, aiming to secure a resilient water future while fostering environmental stewardship and community involvement.

 
Vineyard City Water Conservation Plan
https://conservewater.utah.gov/wp-content/uploads/SubmittedWaterPlans/Water-Conservation-Plan-Vineyard-2022.pdf

item.title: Water Leak Detection and Repairs
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Vineyard City secures its drinking water from wells and various sites in Utah Valley, coordinated through the Central Utah Water Conservancy District (CUWCD) and Orem City. The Vineyard City Public Works oversees the distribution of culinary water to residents and businesses. In response to the city's growth, the Public Works Department strategically manages the delicate balance between limited water resources and the demands of rapid expansion. This includes the implementation of water-efficient fixtures and the promotion of prudent water usage practices among residents and businesses.

 
Residents in Vineyard City can take a proactive approach to water conservation by monitoring and addressing potential leaks in their homes. The EyeOnWater website provides a valuable tool for residents to track their water consumption in real-time, enabling them to detect unusual usage patterns that may indicate leaks. By regularly checking their water usage on the EyeOnWater platform, residents can identify and promptly address leaks, contributing to overall water conservation efforts. This proactive engagement empowers residents to play an active role in ensuring the efficient use of water resources, promoting sustainability, and collectively contributing to the responsible management of Vineyard City's water supply.
 
EyeOnWater, requires your Vineyard City Utility Account information.
https://www.eyeonwater.com/signin

item.title: Water Quality Reports
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Vineyard City ensures safe drinking water by adhering to state and federal regulations, including the Utah Division of Drinking Water standards and the Safe Drinking Water Act enforced by the EPA. The city maintains water quality within acceptable limits through rigorous testing, monitoring, and robust treatment processes. Regular maintenance and infrastructure upgrades are also prioritized to uphold the integrity of the water supply system. In this way, Vineyard City consistently provides clean and safe drinking water to its residents, meeting or exceeding regulatory standards.

item.title: Pay Your Bill
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
There are two ways to pay your bill electronically. Vineyard offers a Direct Pay option where the bill will automatically be taken from your bank account on or around the 20th of each month. You can view and print the Direct Pay Authorization (PDF) online. You can email the completed form to the department. This option is only available for homeowners.

You may also make your utility payments online by setting up your account with XPress Billpay! This is an easy option for renters and those wanting to pay with a credit card. An auto pay option is available through XPress Bill Pay.

Important Note: If you were signed up for Direct Pay and need to update banking info, please call Vineyard City at 801-226-1929. Direct Pay and XPress Bill Pay are two separate entities that do not communicate with each other.

item.title: Privacy Notice
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Vineyard City is committed to protecting your privacy. When the Finance Department requests or collects personal data, this notice is provided in compliance with Utah Code 63A-19-402 to inform you about how your information will be used. 

1. Why the Finance Department Is Requesting Your Personal Data 

The Finance Department collects personal data to deliver Vineyard City services, process applications and reimbursements, invoice for services, rentals, and sponsorships, and coordinate with partner agencies and departments. Providing this information helps the Finance Department efficiently serve you and fulfill governmental responsibilities. 

2. Intended Purposes and Uses of Your Personal Data 

Your personal data will be used for the following purposes:  

  • Process Utility and Hydrant Meter Applications 
  • Process Utility Payments 
  • Manage Eco-Pass enrollment with Utah Transit Authority (UTA) 
  • Administer Recreation and Library reimbursements 
  • Provide address and contact details to support Neighborhood Services and the Sheriff’s Department 
  • Invoice for special services, rentals, and sponsorships 
  • Provide regular notifications and announcements from Vineyard City
3. Consequences of Refusing to Provide Personal Data 


Providing personal data is mandatory for this service. If you choose not to provide the requested information:  

  • Your application will not be processed, and you will be ineligible for city utilities   
4. Data Sharing 


Your personal data may be shared with the following:  

  • Entities that share personal data with the Finance Department: Vineyard’s Building & Planning Departments, the Sheriff’s Department, Public Works Department, Communication Department. 
  • Entities that receive personal data from the Finance Department on a regular or contractual basis: Vineyard Neighborhood Service Coordinator, Communication Department, Sheriff’s Department, Utah Transit Authority (UTA), Zions Bank, CC Bank.
5. Record Series


Personal data collected by the Finance Department will be included in the following record series: 

  • RS2206 
  • RS507
6. Your Rights and Additional Information 


You have the right to request a copy of this notice regarding personal data you previously provided. To request this information or to ask questions about how your data is handled, please contact:  
Vineyard City Privacy Manager  
privacy@vineyardutah.gov  

This notice is available:  

  • At the point of data collection  
  • Upon request  

By providing your personal data, you acknowledge that you have been informed of how your information will be used and shared in accordance with this notice.
